Materials are the input that is both flexible and deductible. Because materials are flexible, the firm's first-order condition equates the share of materials over sales to the output elasticity of materials and output measurement error. If the elasticity were known, the gap between the reported share of materials over sales and the elasticity would measure overreporting, up to the measurement error. This is the materials condition.

Because materials are deductible, every overreported peso lowers a firm's tax bill by the sales-tax rate on purchases. But overreporting is costly. A firm that overreports weighs this benefit against the probability of detection and the cost of overreporting, which include accounting and opportunity costs. This trade-off is the evasion condition.

[This chapter]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}[This section]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"} derives both conditions, which the rest of the [thesis]{.content-hidden when-meta="jmp"}[paper]{.content-visible when-meta="jmp"} builds on. The materials condition (@eq-share-net) underlies the test, the deconvolution, and the production-function estimates (@sec-testing to @sec-pf). The evasion condition (@eq-foc-e) underlies the analysis of the 1983 reform and the counterfactual (@sec-fiscal, @sec-counterfactual).

## Setup

Price-taking firms maximize expected after-tax profits. They share a common technology but differ in productivity. A firm $i$ in year $t$ produces output $Y_{it}$ with capital $K_{it}$, labour $L_{it}$, and materials $M_{it}$,

$$
Y_{it}=K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}).
$$ {#eq-pf}

As in the production-function literature, materials are the flexible input, which the firm adjusts freely each year, while capital and labour are predetermined or dynamic. Productivity, $\omega_{it}$, is known to the firm when it chooses its inputs, so inputs respond to it, which creates the simultaneity problem in estimating production functions [@Griliches1995]. $\varepsilon_{it}$ is measurement error in output.

<!-- Because $\varepsilon_{it}$ is an error in the record of output, not a shock to production, the firm's decisions depend on true output, $K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it})$, and productivity is $\exp(\omega_{it})$. In @Gandhi2020, by contrast, $\varepsilon_{it}$ is a shock to output that the firm does not know when it chooses its inputs. -->

The firm sells its output at price $P_t$ and owes sales tax at rate $\tau_S$ on its sales. It buys materials at price $\rho_t$ and pays a sales tax at rate $\tau_P$, but the firm can deduct the tax paid on them from the tax it owes on sales.

<!-- When the credit exceeds the tax owed, as for firms exempt from the tax on their sales, the tax authority refunds the difference (@sec-setting-incentive).



The model's notation matches the variables of @tbl-sum-stats: output $Y_{it}$, capital $K_{it}$, labour $L_{it}$, reported materials $M^*_{it}$, and the rates $\tau_S$ and $\tau_P$. Lowercase letters denote logs. The econometrician observes reported materials, $M^*_{it}$, but not true materials, $M_{it}$, or overreporting, $e_{it}$. -->



## Expected profit {#sec-exp-prof}

The firm might choose to increase its reported material consumption by $e_{it}$ units to claim additional credits on materials. Firms report $M^*_{it}=M_{it}+e_{it}$. Capital goods and labour expenses cannot be deducted from sales-tax liabilities.

Overreporting is detected with a probability $q(e_{it})$, which increases with the amount overreported. A firm that does not overreport has nothing to hide, and thus its probability of detection is zero, $q(0)=0$. A firm that is caught repays the credit it claimed on $e_{it}$ plus a fine, a multiple $\phi$ of that credit.

Evaders pay a cost of evasion $\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})$. The cost is increasing in the overreported amount, is zero for a firm that does not overreport, $\kappa_{it}(0,\omega_{it})=0$, and is paid whether or not the firm is caught. $\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})$ represents direct costs of overreporting, such as the price of fake invoices, and opportunity costs: any resource reallocated from a productive activity to tax evasion, such as the manager's time.

The cost of evasion depends on productivity, which lets the model match the observed pattern in recent evidence. In Ecuador, the share of firms' deductions backed by receipts from fake firms rises with firm revenue over most of the size distribution but drops sharply at the very top [@Carrillo2022, p. 6]. The probability of detection could not explain this pattern. If allowed to vary with size, it would imply that larger firms overreport more because their probability of detection is lower. This does not make economic sense. Larger firms are more visible to the tax authority, so their probability of detection is, if anything, at least as high as that of smaller firms. Only the drop at the top could come from a higher probability of detection.

In the model, the cost of evasion produces the whole pattern because it is a better candidate to explain the pattern. More productive firms are larger and have more resources to allocate to evasion, and thus their cost of evasion is lower. For the most productive firms, however, the cost rises relative to other tools: they can turn to legal avoidance instead of overreporting, which is illegal [@Carrillo2022, p. 6]. The largest firms also have more to lose if caught, and evading requires more employees to collude [@Almunia2018]. A cost of evasion that falls with productivity over most of the distribution and rises at the top captures both forces. Therefore, I assume a cost of evasion convex in productivity.

Since underreporting inputs would increase the tax liability, no firm has an incentive to do so. Hence $e_{it}\ge0$.

The optimization problem of the firm is then,
$$
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{M,e,K,L}\;\mathbb{E}[\pi_{it}] = \;&(1-\tau_S)P_tK_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it})-(1-\tau_P)\rho_tM_{it}-r_tK_{it}-w_tL_{it}\\
  &+\tau_P\rho_te_{it}\big[1-(1+\phi)q(e_{it})\big]-\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-profit}

The first term is revenue net of the tax on sales; the second, the cost of true materials net of the credit on them; the third and fourth, the rental cost of capital at rate $r_t$ and the wage bill at wage $w_t$. The fifth term is the credit on overreported materials net of the expected repayment and fine, and the last is the cost of evasion.

## First-order conditions

### The materials condition {#sec-model-foc-m}

Taking the first-order condition of @eq-profit with respect to $M_{it}$, we have,

$$
(1-\tau_S)P_t\,\beta K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta-1}\exp(\omega_{it})=(1-\tau_P)\rho_t.
$$ {#eq-foc-m}

@eq-foc-m looks familiar except for the tax wedge: the left-hand side is the marginal revenue product of materials and the right-hand side is the price of materials, both net of taxes.

The taxes matter when $\tau_P\neq\tau_S$. By changing either rate, the government changes the price of materials relative to output, and with it the firm's choice of materials. If $(1-\tau_P)/(1-\tau_S)>1$, materials become more expensive relative to output than without taxes, and the firm uses less of them; if the ratio is below one, as when the rate on purchases exceeds the rate on sales, materials become cheaper and the firm uses more of them.

Multiplying @eq-foc-m by $M_{it}$, dividing by measured output, $P_tY_{it}$, and taking logs gives the log share of materials in output, net of sales taxes:

$$
\ln\left(\frac{(1-\tau_P)\rho_tM_{it}}{(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}}\right)=\ln\beta-\varepsilon_{it}.
$$ {#eq-share-net}

With a single rate, the tax terms cancel and the gross share, $\rho_tM_{it}/P_tY_{it}$, satisfies the same equation as the no-tax optimization condition. The two shares differ little in the data: the log ratio $\ln\big((1-\tau_S)/(1-\tau_P)\big)$ has a standard deviation of 0.05 across firm-years, against 0.34 for the log gross share.

Productivity does not appear in the share. If we knew $\ln\beta$, a deviation of the reported share from it could separate overreporting from productivity. Furthermore, if we knew the moments or the distribution of $\varepsilon_{it}$, then we could estimate moments and properties of the distribution of overreporting. @sec-testing builds on @eq-share-net to identify $\beta$ and to test for overreporting. @sec-deconvolution employs deconvolution techniques to learn about the distribution of overreporting by removing $\varepsilon_{it}$.


### The evasion condition

The first-order condition with respect to $e_{it}$ shows that,

$$
\tau_P\rho_t\big[1-(1+\phi)\big(q(e_{it})+q'(e_{it})e_{it}\big)\big]=\frac{\partial\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})}{\partial e_{it}}.
$$ {#eq-foc-e}

To better understand the incentives to overreport, @eq-foc-e can be rewritten in terms of the elasticity of the probability of detection with respect to overreporting, $\xi_{q,e}=q'(e_{it})e_{it}/q(e_{it})$:

$$
\tau_P\rho_t\big[1-(1+\phi)(1+\xi_{q,e})\,q(e_{it})\big]=\frac{\partial\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})}{\partial e_{it}}.
$$ {#eq-foc-e-elas}

The left-hand side is the marginal benefit of overreporting, and the right-hand side is its marginal cost. The marginal benefit decreases with the fine, $\phi$, the probability of detection, $q(e_{it})$, and the elasticity of the probability of detection, $\xi_{q,e}$.

A higher tax rate on purchases raises overreporting. A higher rate on purchases raises the credit on every fictitious peso, whether or not the firm is caught, so the firm overreports more. By the implicit function theorem, $\partial e^*_{it}/\partial\tau_P>0$ for any probability of detection and cost of evasion that satisfy the second-order condition (@sec-app-soc-model). This sign is the prediction that @sec-fiscal tests with the 1983 reform, and $e^*_{it}(\tau_P)$ is the object that @sec-counterfactual estimates.

Some firms choose not to overreport at all. For them, the marginal cost of evasion exceeds the marginal benefit at any positive level of overreporting, so @eq-foc-e does not hold with equality; instead, at $e_{it}=0$,

$$
\tau_P\rho_t\le\frac{\partial\kappa_{it}(0,\omega_{it})}{\partial e_{it}}.
$$ {#eq-foc-noeva}

Firms that pay no tax on their purchases ($\tau_P=0$) are always in this group.

The model allows the two rates to differ, as they do in the data. Firms sell and buy goods taxed at different rates, and the two rates differ by more than one percentage point in 56 percent of firm-years. But the two rates might be equal, $\tau_S=\tau_P=\tau$ (@sec-app-single-tax). In that case, the first-order condition of materials would not have a tax wedge and the single rate would replace $\tau_P$ in @eq-foc-e.

### Corporations

Corporations are corner firms by assumption. They share the technology of the other firms and may differ in productivity, but audited statements and scrutiny by government and markets keep them from overreporting (@sec-setting-jo). I assume that @eq-foc-noeva always holds for them. For other firms, a corner solution follows from $\kappa_{it}$, $\omega_{it}$, and $\tau_P$. For corporations, $e_{it}=0$ is a constraint, and I use them only as the truth-reporting benchmark. Corporations may still overreport a little: in Ecuador, the tax evaded through fake receipts amounted to 1.7 percent for corporations, against 11.5 percent for sole proprietorships [@Carrillo2022, p. 6]. If Colombian corporations also overreport a little, my estimates understate the overreporting of unincorporated firms and are a lower bound.

## Relation to other work

The model departs from standard production-function methods that depend on the flexible input [@Levinsohn2003; @Doraszelski2013; @Ackerberg2015; @Gandhi2020] in two ways. First, true materials are unobserved. Second, firms pay sales taxes. This matters because, if the rate on sales differs from the rate on purchases, the taxes change the price of materials relative to output. Hence, the government can indirectly influence how much material the firm uses and thus real output (@sec-model-foc-m).

Regarding the firm's evasion decision in the tradition of @Allingham1972, @Almunia2018 sit close to the model presented in this section. I depart from them in three ways. First, the firm overreports a deductible input under a sales tax that credits purchases, rather than underreporting revenue under a tax on profits. Second, the probability of detection does not jump when the firm's reported revenue crosses a threshold. Colombia had no discontinuity in the probability of detection we could exploit. Third, the cost of evasion varies with the firm's productivity, as explained before in this section (@sec-exp-prof).

I focus on overreported inputs rather than underreported sales because underreporting sales is harder for firms that sell to other firms, as Colombian manufacturers mostly did. First, sales between firms leave a thicker paper trail than sales to consumers. Consumers do not always ask for invoices, whereas firms require invoices so they can deduct their purchases [@Slemrod2019, pp. 925--927]. Second, seller and buyer firms face opposing incentives, which renders coordination between them unlikely: the seller gains from underreporting the sale, but the buyer gains from overreporting the purchase. In a 1984 survey, Colombian manufacturers sold 13 percent of their production directly to the public, about 20 percent to retailers, and most of the rest to wholesalers [@Perry1990, pp. 183--184, table 16-3]. Focusing on Colombian manufacturers between 1981 and 1991 therefore lets me study input overreporting largely separately from sales underreporting.
